You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.02 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.15 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.01 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 4 of 12.

RESULTS OF YOUR PREVIOUS ROUND:

Design 1 'Symmetric_SECE': duplicate: same structure as an earlier design (SyncBoost_Rectifier); nothing new was simulated. Values are tuned automatically, so propose a different structure.

BEST DESIGNS SO FAR (values already tuned):

[c0018] SSHI_FullBridge  (topology 40eae91a637a, score 19.41, conditions passed 0/6)
D1 D pzp out DSCH
D2 D pzn out DSCH
D3 D 0 pzp DSCH
D4 D 0 pzn DSCH
L1 L pzp n1 0.00785
S1 S n1 pzn ctrl=G1
G1 SYNC ton=7.48e-05s phase=0.0641 edges=both
C1 C out 0 4.16e-07
Dz D 0 out DZ33
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.76    2.79    67.2  0.0438      23.1  ok       ok       FAIL     ok       ok      
S2       2.04    2.07    91.9  0.0638      27.6  ok       ok       FAIL     ok       ok      
S3       3.38    3.42      88  0.0169      5.18  ok       ok       FAIL     ok       ok      
S4       1.98    1.99    21.2   0.124      3.91  ok       ok       FAIL     ok       ok

S6       2.86    2.89    75.2  0.0438      24.8  ok       ok       FAIL     ok       ok      
failing: S2 ripple: 0.09193 V (needs <= 0.02 V, margin -3.60)
S3 ripple: 0.08799 V (needs <= 0.02 V, margin -3.40)

value sizing: 48/48 evaluations (finished: budget used)
what this means:
- ripple is too large on S1 (67 mV), S2 (92 mV), S3 (88 mV) and 3 more: the storage cannot buffer the charge pulses against the load

Topologies explored so far (hash: name, best score):
  40eae91a637a: SSHI_FullBridge (19.41)

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: $V_{out\_min} \ge 1.8V$, $V_{out\_max} \le 3.6V$, Ripple $V_{pp} \le 0.02V$, $t_{up} \le 0.15s$, Settled $\Delta v \le 0.01V$.
    *   Previous Best: `SSHI_FullBridge`.
    *   Current Issues: Ripple is too high (63-92 mV), whereas the limit is 20 mV.
    *   Observations: All other metrics ($V_{avg}$, $V_{max}$, $t_{up}$, settled) are "ok" or very close.
    *   Cause of ripple: The storage capacitor $C_1$ is too small ($416\text{ nF}$). In the current topology, the charge pulses from the SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor) stage are hitting the output capacitor, and the load $R_L$ (which varies from $150\text{ k}\Omega$ to $2200\text{ k}\Omega$) cannot smooth the ripple enough with a $416\text{ nF}$ cap.

    *   The ripple $\Delta V \approx \frac{I_{peak} \cdot \Delta t}{C_{out}}$.
    *   To reduce ripple, we need a larger $C_{out}$.
    *   However, the budget for $C$ is $4.7\mu\text{F}$. The current value is $0.416\mu\text{F}$.
    *   Wait, the previous result says "value sizing: 48/48 evaluations (finished)". This means the evolution strategy already tried to optimize $C_1$ within its allowed range ($100\text{ pF}$ to $4.7\mu\text{F}$). If it settled on $416\text{ nF}$ and still had ripple, it might be because increasing $C$ slowed down the startup time $t_{up}$ or affected the settled mean.
    *   Actually, looking at the results: $t_{up}$ is $0.0169$ to $0.124\text{ s}$, which is well within the $0.15\text{ s}$ limit. So there's room to increase $C_1$ to $4.7\mu\text{F}$ if the optimizer didn't. But the optimizer is supposed to find the best value. If it stopped at $416\text{ nF}$, maybe it's due to the objective function.

    *   The SSHI circuit usually involves an inductor and a switch to flip the voltage across $C_p$ at the peaks.
    *   Current `SSHI_FullBridge` uses:
        *   Full bridge (D1-D4)
        *   $L_1$ and $S_1$ (SYNC)
        *   $C_1$ (output)
        *   $D_z$ (zener clamp)
    *   Topology: Piezo terminals $\rightarrow$ Bridge $\rightarrow$ Out. The $L_1-S_1$ is connected to $pzp$ and $pzn$.
    *   Wait, the components provided for `SSHI_FullBridge` are:
        `D1: pzp out`, `D2: pzn out`, `D3: 0 pzp`, `D4: 0 pzn`. This is a standard full bridge.
        `L1: pzp n1`, `S1: n1 pzn`. This connects $L_1$ in series with $S_1$ across the piezo terminals. This is the classic SECE (Synchronized Electric Charge Extraction) or SSHI-style inversion loop.

    *   The ripple is the only failing metric. $V_{avg}$ is well above $1.8\text{V}$ (except for S4 where it's $1.98\text{V}$).
    *   The current structure is quite efficient (it's an SSHI/SECE hybrid).
    *   If ripple is the issue, we might need a way to filter the output or improve the charge delivery.
    *   Alternatively, perhaps a different rectifier stage? The full bridge has 2 diode drops.
    *   What if we use a charge pump or a different switching strategy?
    *   Let's look at the $L-C$ resonance. The $L_1-S_1$ loop flips $V_{Cp}$ to move charge more efficiently.
    *   To reduce ripple, we can try a larger capacitor, but the optimizer should have done that. Let's double-check if there's any other way to smooth the output.
    *   Maybe an LC filter? But we only have 16 components.
    *   Let's try a "Parallel SSHI" or a "Synchronous Rectifier" approach.
    *   Actually, if the current topology is almost perfect except for ripple, and the optimizer didn't just max out $C_1$, we should consider if the charge pulses are too large or too infrequent.
    *   Wait, the $V_{pp}$ is $60-90\text{ mV}$. This is actually quite low for a piezo harvester. The target is $20\text{ mV}$.
    *   Increasing $C_{out}$ is the direct way to solve this. If the optimizer didn't go to $4.7\mu\text{F}$, it's strange. But maybe the energy delivered per pulse is high, and the time between pulses is $5\text{ms}$ (100Hz, both edges).

    *   Could a capacitor-based SSHI (instead of inductor-based) work? No, inductor-based is usually more efficient.
    *   What about a "SyncBoost" where the switch is part of the boost converter?
    *   Let's try a different approach for the rectification:
        Instead of a full bridge, use a half-bridge with a center-tapped source? No, the piezo is a current source.
        What about a synchronous rectifier? (Using switches instead of diodes).
    *   Wait, I only have 4 switches.
    *   Let's try a "Buck-Boost" like structure for the output.
    *   Actually, let's look at the "Symmetric SECE" or "SSHI" again.
    *   The current design has the inductor $L_1$ in parallel with the piezo. When $S_1$ closes, $L_1$ and $C_p$ exchange energy, flipping the voltage. This increases the voltage at the piezo terminals, allowing more charge to flow through the bridge.
    *   To reduce ripple, maybe we can use a different storage method. Or perhaps the inductor should be in series with the output?
    *   Let's try the "Standard SECE" topology:
        Piezo $\rightarrow$ Rectifier $\rightarrow$ $L_{out}$ $\rightarrow$ $C_{out}$.
        Wait, the SECE topology typically involves the inductor $L$ being switched *after* the rectifier or in a way that it acts as a current source.

    *   Proposed Topology: **SECE with output Inductor**
        1.  Piezo $\rightarrow$ Full Bridge (D1-D4).
        2.  Bridge output (node `rect_out`) $\rightarrow$ Inductor $L_1 \rightarrow$ node `out`.
        3.  Switch $S_1$ from `rect_out` to `0`. (This is the SECE switch).
        4.  Storage $C_1$ at node `out`.
        5.  Zener $D_z$ at node `out`.

    *   How it works:
        *   During the "open" phase, charge flows from the piezo through the bridge and $L_1$ into $C_1$.
        *   At the peak, $S_1$ closes, shorting the bridge output to ground. This allows the inductor $L_1$ to dump its energy into $C_1$ while the piezo is essentially shorted or recharging.
        *   This typically produces a more continuous current into $C_1$ than the full-bridge alone, potentially reducing ripple.

    *   Alternative Topology: **Active Rectifier (Synchronous)**
        *   Use switches $S_1, S_2$ instead of $D_1, D_2$ for the top part of the bridge.
        *   This reduces the voltage drop (improving $V_{avg}$) and might change the ripple characteristics.
        *   But we need a controller for each switch.

    *   Let's refine the **SECE-like structure**:
        *   $D_1: pzp \rightarrow n_{rect}$
        *   $D_2: pzn \rightarrow n_{rect}$
        *   $D_3: 0 \rightarrow pzp$
        *   $D_4: 0 \rightarrow pzn$
        *   $L_1: n_{rect} \rightarrow out$
        *   $S_1: n_{rect} \rightarrow 0$
        *   $C_1: out \rightarrow 0$
        *   $D_z: 0 \rightarrow out$ (Zener)
        *   $G_1: SYNC$ controlling $S_1$.

    *   Actually, let's look at the `SSHI_FullBridge` results again. The $V_{avg}$ is great. The $V_{max}$ is great. Only the ripple is failing.
    *   If $V_{pp} = 80\text{ mV}$ and we need $20\text{ mV}$, we need a $4\times$ increase in $C_{out}$ (if $C$ is the dominant factor).
    *   $416\text{ nF} \times 4 = 1.66\mu\text{F}$. This is well within the $4.7\mu\text{F}$ limit.
    *   Why didn't the optimizer use it?
        Maybe the optimizer's cost function penalized the startup time $t_{up}$?
        $t_{up}$ for S4 was $0.124\text{ s}$, and the limit is $0.15\text{ s}$. If $C$ increases to $1.6\mu\text{F}$, $t_{up}$ will likely exceed $0.15\text{ s}$.
    *   This is the trade-off: Larger $C$ $\rightarrow$ Lower Ripple, but Slower Startup.
    *   To solve this, we need a topology that charges $C_{out}$ faster *and* maintains low ripple.

    *   A "Boost" converter can provide a higher voltage and potentially charge the cap faster.
    *   But we have a piezo (current source).
    *   Wait, the `SSHI_FullBridge` is already doing a form of voltage boosting (the $L-C$ inversion).
    *   What if we use a **Synchronous Rectifier** to reduce diode drops?
        $D_1$ and $D_2$ (the ones going to $out$) are the main bottlenecks for startup.
        Replacing $D_1$ with $S_1$ and $D_2$ with $S_2$ would remove the $0.25\text{V}$ drop.
        Wait, the SYNC controller can only trigger at peaks. A synchronous rectifier needs to be on for half a cycle. The SYNC controller `ton` is max $1\text{ms}$. A half-cycle at $100\text{Hz}$ is $5\text{ms}$. So the SYNC controller cannot be used as a standard rectifier switch.

    *   Let's try the **SECE (Synchronized Electric Charge Extraction)** topology again.
        In SECE, the inductor $L$ is not in parallel with the piezo; it's between the rectifier and the storage.
        This allows the energy from $C_p$ to be extracted more efficiently and delivered in a more controlled pulse.

    *   Let's try another structure: **Parallel SSHI with a larger C and a slightly different L placement**.
        Wait, what if we use the `S1` switch to short the piezo *directly*?
        No, let's try the SECE:
        - Bridge: `D1(pzp, n1), D2(pzn, n1), D3(0, pzp), D4(0, pzn)`
        - $L_1$: `n1` to `out`
        - $S_1$: `n1` to `0` (ctrl: G1)
        - $C_1$: `out` to `0`
        - $D_z$: `0` to `out`

    *   Let's think about the ripple again. $V_{pp} \le 20\text{ mV}$.
        If the optimizer cannot increase $C_{out}$ because of $t_{up}$, we need to increase the *average current* delivered during startup or find a way to reduce the pulse magnitude.
        The current `SSHI_FullBridge` uses a full bridge. The $L-S$ loop is across the piezo.
        This means the inductor is used to flip $V_{Cp}$, but the charge still has to go through the bridge.

    *   Let's try a **Voltage Doubler** (Dickson charge pump style) but using the piezo's nature.
        Actually, for piezos, a "Half-Bridge" with a capacitor and an inductor often works well.

    *   Let's try a **Simplified SSHI** (without the full bridge) to see if we can get faster startup.
        Piezo terminals $pzp, pzn$.
        $D_1: pzp \rightarrow out$
        $S_1: pzp \rightarrow pzn$ (controlled by G1)
        $C_1: out \rightarrow 0$
        This only harvests half the cycle.

    *   Let's go back to the **SECE** (Synchronized Electric Charge Extraction) topology.
        SECE is known for being very efficient and having a relatively fast startup.
        Circuit:
        1.  Full bridge (D1-D4) $\rightarrow$ node `n1`.
        2.  $L_1$ from `n1` to `out`.
        3.  $S_1$ from `n1` to `0` (ctrl: G1, edges: both).
        4.  $C_1$ from `out` to `0`.
        5.  $D_z$ from `0` to `out`.

        Wait, the "Symmetric SECE" was already tried (hash `fcb6f6a8b4de`). Let's check if this is the same.
        Symmetric SECE usually means the inductor is shifted.
        Let's try a **modified SECE** where $L_1$ is in series with the piezo and $S_1$ is used differently.
        Actually, let's try a **SyncBoost** but with a more optimized arrangement.

    *   What if we use a **Low-Pass Filter** at the output?
        $L_{out}$ from `n1` to `out`, $C_{out}$ from `out` to `0`.
        Wait, the SECE already has this. $L_1$ is from `n1` to `out`.
        The difference is the switch $S_1$.

    *   Let's try the **SSHI-FullBridge** again, but with a different inductor placement to see if we can reduce the ripple without sacrificing startup.
        Wait, the only way to reduce ripple is to increase $C_{out}$ or reduce the pulse current.
        If $t_{up}$ is the limiting factor for $C_{out}$, we need to increase the current during startup.
        How to increase current?
        - Reduce diode drops. (Impossible with the given SYNC controller).
        - Increase the voltage at the piezo terminals. (The SSHI loop already does this).

    *   Wait! I have an idea. What if I use a **Parallel Capacitor** to buffer the charge before the output capacitor?
        No, that just increases the total capacitance.

    *   Let's try a **modified bridge** where the zener $D_z$ is not just a clamp but helps in the process? No.

    *   Let's try a **C-L-S (Capacitor-Inductor-Switch)** network that delivers charge more smoothly.
        What if $S_1$ doesn't short the bridge, but instead connects a second inductor? No, only 16 components.

    *   Let's try the **SSHI** but instead of a full bridge, we use a **Half-Bridge with a storage capacitor**?
        $D_1: pzp \rightarrow out$
        $D_2: pzn \rightarrow out$ (wait, that's not possible)

    *   Let's try: **Inductor-based SSHI with a different switch position**.
        Current: $L_1$ and $S_1$ in parallel with the piezo.
        New: $L_1$ in series with the piezo, $S_1$ switching $L_1$ to ground? No.

    *   Let's try: **The "Standard" SECE** again, but be very careful with the connectivity.
        D1: pzp, n1
        D2: pzn, n1
        D3: 0, pzp
        D4: 0, pzn
        L1: n1, out
        S1: n1, 0
        C1: out, 0
        Dz: 0, out
        G1: edges=both, phase=0.0

        This structure is designed to deliver the energy of $C_p$ to $C_{out}$ via $L_1$ in a more controlled manner.
        The charge is accumulated in $L_1$ and then dumped.

    *   Another attempt: **Modified SSHI with an LC output filter**.
        D1: pzp, n1
        D2: pzn, n1
        D3: 0, pzp
        D4: 0, pzn
        L1: n1, out
        C1: out, 0
        L2: n2, n1 (Wait, too many components)

    *   Let's try **one more SSHI variant**:
        Instead of the full bridge, use two diodes and the SYNC switch to create a half-wave rectifier with inversion.
        S1: pzp, pzn (ctrl: G1)
        D1: pzp, out
        C1: out, 0
        Dz: 0, out
        (This is too simple, probably won't meet $V_{avg}$ for S4).

    *   Let's look at the `SSHI_FullBridge` failing again.
        S4 is the most critical for $V_{avg}$ (1.98V, just above 1.8V) and $t_{up}$ (0.124s, just below 0.15s).
        The ripple is the only failure.
        If we increase $C_1$ to $1\mu\text{F}$ for S4, $t_{up}$ will increase by $1\mu\text{F} / 416\text{nF} \approx 2.4\times$.
        $0.124\text{s} \times 2.4 = 0.3\text{s}$. This fails the $0.15\text{s}$ limit.
        So we MUST increase the current during startup to allow for a larger $C_1$.

    *   How to increase startup current?
        The current is limited by the diode drops and the piezo's current source.
        $I_{avg} \approx \frac{2 \cdot C_p \cdot \Delta V \cdot f}{1}$.
        To increase $I_{avg}$, we need to increase $\Delta V$ (the voltage swing across $C_p$).
        The SSHI loop (L1, S1) already increases $\Delta V$ by flipping the voltage.
        Can we increase it more?
        The current flip is $V_{pzp} \rightarrow -V_{pzp}$. The total swing is $2 \cdot V_{pzp}$.
        This is the maximum possible for a simple inductor flip.

    *   What if we use a **different rectifier**?
        The current bridge is:
        D1: pzp, out
        D2: pzn, out
        D3: 0, pzp
        D4: 0, pzn
        This is a full bridge.
        What if we use a **Center-Tapped Rectifier**?
        We don't have a center tap, but we can create one using a capacitor.
        $C_{mid}$ between $pzp$ and $pzn$.
